uncited: It sets itself apart from static mapping strategies by dynamically redistributing work and organizing computation to minimize global atomic updates, replacing them with local reductions or cache-cooperative operations.
**Dynamic Work Redistribution:** Static mappings of Gaussians to tiles or pixels are prone to warp divergence due to footprint coverage and early termination.
**Local Gradient Reduction:** Backward propagation requires accumulating gradients from many pixels into each Gaussian.

Instead of performing frequent global atomic updates, these methods organize computation to combine gradients locally (within a warp, tile, or Gaussian-centric block) before writing the final result back to global memory.
The concept emerged as a response to the inefficiencies of static rasterization schedules in 3D Gaussian Splatting.
